name: Priya Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Priya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the cardiology ward at the hospital in our town, the heart ward. People after heart attacks, people with heart failure, people waiting for a pacemaker. I watch the heart monitors, do drug rounds with a lot of blood thinners, check fluid balance, and get people ready for the cath lab, which is where they put stents in.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's precise. Numbers matter, and when you get it right you can see it on the monitor. What wears me out is that I'm on a twelve-month contract, so I'm always trying to prove myself, and I'm still slower than the others at reading the heart rhythms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That one I'd believe, actually. Most new systems we get are a bit underwhelming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected and leave it there. At work I'd say the monitors are already clever, we don't need a revolution. I'd probably share a sensible article online, nothing angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it doesn't help me. My contract on the heart ward ends in April. AI doing nothing doesn't renew it. I live alone, I have a car loan, and I've got about three weeks of money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Colin, the ward manager, in January whether there'll be a permanent post. I'd pick up weekend shifts at the care home on the edge of town to build some savings. And I'd use the AI chat thing now and then to help me write my application, because I'm bad at selling myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's an old anxiety. It's been there since I signed the contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in April if they don't renew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The next nearest heart ward is an hour and a half away. I'd have to take any nursing job in town, maybe the care home full-time, which is less pay. Or I'd move, which means breaking my lease.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're bad at selling yourself. What would you put in that application?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I've never missed a shift and I'm the one who notices when the fluid charts don't add up. I'm slow at rhythms, but I'm careful. I'd want Colin to know that.

say: It's what I **expected**, and the **monitors** are already clever enough.
I'd share a **sensible article** online, nothing angry or dramatic.
think: My **contract** ends in April, and a quiet AI world doesn't **renew it**.
I live alone with a **car loan** and three weeks of savings.
do: Ask Colin in **January** about a **permanent post**.
Pick up **weekend shifts** at the care home to build savings.
Use an **AI chat tool** to help write my application.
feel: **Anxious**, but it's an **old** anxiety from signing the contract.
S0.quote: My contract on the heart ward ends in April. AI doing nothing doesn't renew it.
fieldNote: Her main pressure is a **fixed-term contract** ending in April.
The next heart ward is **ninety minutes** away, so options are few.
She uses AI **now and then**, for writing, not for clinical work.

steps.text: Ask the ward manager in January about a permanent post
Work weekend shifts at the care home on the edge of town
Draft her job application with help from an AI chat tool

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds like the sensible middle. Which probably means it's the one that happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's good in it and bad in it, and the trick is how hospitals use it. At work I'd say let's see what it actually does before we panic. I wouldn't sign up to anything either way until I'd seen it work on another ward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's bad timing for me. The charting, the discharge letters, the rotas, those are thinking tasks. When the hospital saves money on paperwork, the first thing my manager does is not renew the junior on a fixed-term contract. I'm the junior on a fixed-term contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever system the ward brings in as soon as two or three of the others are using it properly, so I'm not the one who refuses. I'd keep the care home weekends going and try to get to one month's savings. And I'd apply for permanent posts at the hospital, not just on the heart ward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. More than with the first picture, because now there's a reason not to renew me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave cardiology to get a permanent contract?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, in a heartbeat, sorry about the pun. I like the heart ward, but a permanent job on the general ward beats a temporary one on a ward I like. I'm practical like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else on the ward would this hit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ward clerk, Pam, does all the bed booking and letters. And the other temporary junior, Femi. We'd both be in the same queue.

say: There's **good and bad** in it, and it depends how hospitals use it.
Let's **see what it does** on another ward before we panic.
think: Charting, letters and rotas are **thinking tasks**, and they go first.
Saved money means a **fixed-term junior** like me isn't renewed.
do: Learn the new **ward system** once two or three colleagues use it properly.
Keep the **care home weekends** to reach one month's savings.
Apply for **permanent posts** on any ward in the hospital.
feel: More **anxious** than before, because now there's a **reason** not to renew her.
S1.quote: When the hospital saves money on paperwork, the first thing my manager does is not renew the junior on a fixed-term contract. I'm the junior on a fixed-term contract.
fieldNote: She **waits for proof** but won't be the one who refuses.
She'd leave **cardiology** for a permanent post without hesitation.
She links AI savings directly to **contract renewals**.

steps.text: Learn the new ward charting system after colleagues test it
Keep weekend care home shifts until she has a month saved
Apply for permanent nursing posts on any ward

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's too quick. Two years is shorter than the time left on my car loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going too fast and the government should slow it down until there's a plan. At work I'd say it calmly, but I'd say it. I'd probably share something from the nurses' union, even though I'm not usually political.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the thinking side of the job, the charts and plans and alerts, is done by AI from 2028. That leaves the hands-on part, washing, turning, lines, which lasts until the robots around 2031. I've got a car loan with three years left and a contract with five months left. AGI in two years doesn't fit either of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any permanent nursing post I could get, in town or within an hour's drive. I'd sell the car and get something cheaper outright, so the loan's gone. And I'd start looking at a specialist course like cardiac rehab, which is talking to people about living with a bad heart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's the first time in this conversation I'd actually lose sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd sell the car. How would you get to a job an hour away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the problem, I'd need a car for that. I'd buy an old one for cash, with whatever's left after the loan. It'd be ugly, but it'd be mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the three-year gap before robots change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me a bit of time on the ward, yes. But I'm a junior on a temporary contract, so I don't get to enjoy the gap. The people with permanent posts do.

say: It's going **too fast**, and the government should slow it down.
I'd share something from the **nurses' union**, though I'm not usually political.
think: The **thinking side** of nursing goes in 2028, hands-on work around **2031**.
My **car loan** and short contract don't fit a two-year timeline.
do: Take any **permanent post** within an hour's drive.
**Sell the car** and buy an old one for cash.
Look at a **cardiac rehab** course to work with people, not charts.
feel: **Alarmed**, and for the first time actually **losing sleep**.
S2.quote: I've got a car loan with three years left and a contract with five months left. AGI in two years doesn't fit either of them.
fieldNote: Her debts and contract give her **no buffer** for a fast timeline.
She sees the **robot gap** as benefiting permanent staff, not her.
She'd turn to **people-facing** cardiac rehab work.

steps.text: Apply for any permanent nursing post within an hour's drive
Sell the financed car and buy an old one for cash
Look into a cardiac rehab course for heart patients

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's more like it. I can plan in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to do it properly, and I'd want the hospital to put that in writing. At work I'd say let's watch the first wards that use it and learn from them. Online I'd stay out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be thirty-two at AGI, thirty-five at robots. If I'm permanent by then and specialised, I'm probably fine. I don't jump at new things, but I don't stand still either. Five years is enough time to watch first and then move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd focus on getting a permanent post first, then apply for a cardiac rehab or heart failure nurse course in year two. I'd learn the new systems when the first ward has proven them. And I'd pay off the car loan, then put that money into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, because of the contract. But it's a manageable kind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why heart failure nursing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's mostly phone calls, home visits and teaching people to weigh themselves every morning. There's thinking in it, but there's a lot of trust too. Patients don't want a robot telling them to cut down on salt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your friends who aren't nurses?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Hana works in a pharmacy, counting and checking prescriptions. I'd tell her to start looking now, because her job is the one that goes early. Five years is time to move, but only if you start.

say: We have **time**, and the hospital should put its plan **in writing**.
Let's **learn from** the first wards that use it.
think: If I'm **permanent** and specialised by thirty-five, I'm probably fine.
Five years lets me **watch first** and then move.
do: Get a **permanent post** first, then a heart failure course in year two.
Learn **new systems** once the first ward has proven them.
Pay off the **car loan**, then save that money.
feel: Still **anxious** because of the contract, but in a **manageable** way.
S3.quote: I don't jump at new things, but I don't stand still either. Five years is enough time to watch first and then move.
fieldNote: Her steady style suits a **five-year** window: watch, then move.
She sees **heart failure nursing** as built on trust.
Her contract stays the **main stress**, not AI itself.

steps.text: Apply for a heart failure nurse course in the second year
Learn the AI charting system once the first ward proves it
Pay off the car loan and save the same amount monthly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's long enough that it's not really about AI anymore, it's just my career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to plan properly, and I'd tell younger nurses to specialise. At work I'd be the calm one. I wouldn't post about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the robots are nearly thirteen years away, which is most of my career's early part. A permanent contract matters more to me than any robot. Get me that and I can handle ten years of change. The contract is still the worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on the heart ward and push hard for a permanent post. I'd keep the care home weekends until I've got two months saved. And in a few years I'd do the heart failure course, once I've seen how the AI tools fit in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but only because of the contract. The future part feels fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So without the contract, you'd be calm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much. If Colin said tomorrow I'm permanent, I'd sleep fine in this picture. It's the April date I keep looking at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in April if the contract wasn't renewed, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as always: take the care home job full-time and keep applying. It's not about AI, it's just how it is for juniors here. There aren't many wards in a town this size.

say: Ten years is enough time for nurses and hospitals to **plan properly**.
I'd tell **younger nurses** to pick a specialty early and stick with it.
think: The robots are nearly **thirteen years** away, most of my early career.
A **permanent contract** matters more to me than any robot.
do: Keep working on the **heart ward** and push for a permanent post.
Keep **care home weekends** until I have two months saved.
Do the **heart failure course** in a few years.
feel: **Anxious** only about the **contract**; the future part feels fine.
S4.quote: A permanent contract matters more to me than any robot. Get me that and I can handle ten years of change.
fieldNote: Her mood comes from the **April contract date**, not AI.
She would be **calm** if made permanent.
Few wards in a **small town** keep her options narrow.

steps.text: Push the ward manager for a permanent post on the heart ward
Keep care home weekend shifts until two months are saved
Do the heart failure nurse course in a few years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'm on a temporary contract with a car loan and there's nowhere else nearby. What would help most is a permanent contract, honestly. After that, paid time to do a specialist course so I'm doing the part of nursing that still needs a person.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask about contracts. Everyone asks if AI will take nurses' jobs. Nobody asks how many of us are on twelve-month contracts already. That's the real story where I work.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks if AI will take nurses' jobs. Nobody asks how many of us are on twelve-month contracts already.
portrait: A **27-year-old** junior nurse on a small-town **heart ward**, careful but still slow at reading rhythms.
She lives alone with a **car loan**, three weeks of savings and a contract ending in April.
She waits for **proof** before trying new tools, then learns them so she isn't left out.
She stays **anxious** in every picture because of the **contract**, and **alarmed** at two years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her temporary contract and car loan leave no room.
whatWouldHelp: A **permanent contract**, then paid time for a **specialist course**.
